I promise the good that I will never run away any more if they let me out. Please Mr. Barton let me out before I die in this dirty place and I will never run away any more. Daniel Johnson Kasaan Alaska 4/12, 1920 H E Hammonds Sept Cushman agency Tacoma Wash. Dear Sir, I am in receipt of a letter from my Boy Daniel in which he says that you requested him to ask me for money to come home out. He also says that the Cushman School will not run after this year. If such is the case, where would you suggest that I send him to next season, as I want him to go to school somewhere. I wish you would write me, and let me know, if the boy is really in bad shape, I am sending him a check for $100 to come home out. I wish you would see that he gets a ticket, and caution him about spending any of the money unnecessarily. I was greatly in hopes that he would get his full 3 years' time in at the Cushman School. Yours Truly, J F Johnston Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., April 9, 1920 Mr. T. F. Johnson Kasaan, Alaska. Dear Sir: I have to advise you that your son, Daniel, recently had the measles, and it has left him with weak eyes. As a consequence he has been unable to attend school for the past two months. He is becoming somewhat restless and has expressed a desire several times to go home. I told him to write you in regard to the matter and get your advice. Daniel was in my office this morning and expressed his desire to go in the city of Tacoma and get a position. I advised him that I would see the physician and see whether he would be able to return to the school room and also write you and explain matters. I told Daniel that I did not feel as though I could give permission for him to leave the premises without some word from you. Please advise me if you desire him to come home during the summer or continue at the school. This school will be permanently closed in June and it will be necessary to transfer the pupils to either the Tulalip School, near Everett, Washington, or to the Chemawa School, near Salem, Oregon. I would suggest Tulalip as it is nearer his home. Tulalip is a splendid school and he can get just as good schooling there as here. Please advise me at your earliest convenience your desire in this matter and if you want Daniel to come home, send the necessary funds for his transportation. Very truly yours, Special Agent in Charge. CVP:MG Kasaan Alaska Dec 25 1919 Mr E H Hammond Superintendent Indian School Tacoma Wash Dear Sir, Am in receipt of your letter of Nov 21, am pleased to hear my boy is again at school, and I hope that you see that he stays there. I would like to put him through college. If he will attend to his studies at Cushman, I would also be please to help him finish up his education by putting him through some special course of learning, anything that he may choose. But, unless he does get in and study now, he can't expect to get through college or get any special course of training either. I wish you would point out those facts to him. Am enclosing check for $5000 repayment for 3 months services. Yours truly, J F Johnson Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Jan. 7, 1920 Daniel Franklin Johnson Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington My Friend: I have just received a letter from your father in which he says that he is pleased to hear of your progress in your school work. He is very much interested in your making good grades in your studies and that you will continue to progress in your school work and finish your education so far as the Indian Schools will carry you. It is his earnest desire that you learn thoroughly all that this school has to offer so that you may be able to enter College. He is willing to help you in a financial way to secure a special training. It is a fine opportunity for you and I am sure that you have the ability to make the progress in your school work that your father so earnestly desires. Your friend, Special Agent in Charge. OHK:MG Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Jan. 7, 1920 T. F. Johnson Kasaan, Alaska Sir: Enclosed herewith Official Receipt No. 176144, covering tuition in the amount of $50.00 for Daniel F. Johnson. Very respectfully, Special Agent in Charge. :MG Enc. Mr. E. H. Hammonds Sept Cushman Indian School Dear Sir: Am in receipt of your letter and receipt for $20 which I sent you on Oct 14th. You made no mention in regard to my Boy, Is he in school at present or not? I was informed that he was seen in Seattle about Sept 15th, and that he was working on some Gas Boat. I was surprised to learn that he was not at school, as I felt sure that the Present Term of School had Begun Before Sept 15th, and I was also surprised that you said nothing about him. In your note of Oct 21st I kindly advise me fully in regard to this matter. Yours Truly, T. F. Johnson Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Nov. 21, 1919 Mr. T. F. Johnson Kasaan, Alaska Dear Mr. Johnson: Daniel Franklin Johnson was in school at the time the receipt was mailed you October first. During the summer months Daniel was given permission with other large boys to work in the Puyallup Valley to earn spending money. He returned at the re-opening of school and remained in school for a week or so when he again tried to reach Alaska, but was headed off at Seattle and forced to return after a week's absence. This was his third and last attempt. I had a long talk with him and told him that since he would not listen to me he would have to be court-martialed by the student-body. The Battalion officers did court-martial him and sentenced him to go to school and to the Industrial Departments under guard and to sleep in Jail one month. I approved this sentence but after a week I pardoned Daniel and his comrade as they both had decided that it was better to do what was right. Since then Daniel has been working hard. I gave him a five-weeks course in shoe and harness repairing, which he enjoyed and in which he did some very excellent work. He has been detailed to the Engineering Department, in which he is particularly interested. His work in this department is creditable. His instructor is taking an interest in him and if Daniel will give heed to our advice and our instruction, he will not regret the time that he spent at Cushman. He is well and much stouter than when he came to school. I will have him write you himself if he has not done so. This form must be executed in duplicate when a child is transferred from a reservation to a nonreservation school. The Superintendent of the nonreservation school will retain the original for his files, and the duplicate shall be deposited in the reservation school records. The reservation superintendent should send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate as provided by law. All the blanks must be properly filled in every case. If the information called for on any part of the blank is not known, that fact should be stated. No space should be left unfilled. Whether the parents are living or dead, their names must be given. The person who signs the blank as consenting to the transfer should indicate his relation to the applicant by marking out the word "parent," "guardian," or "next of kin," leaving unmarked only the title appropriate to the signer. INDORSEMENTS. Applicable laws relating to the transfer of Indian children from reservations and schools are as follows: That hereafter no Indian child shall be sent from any Indian reservation to a school beyond the State or Territory in which said reservation is situated without the voluntary consent of the father or mother of such child if either of them are living, and if neither of them are living without the voluntary consent of the next of kin of such child. Such consent shall be made before the agent of the reservation, and he shall send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate that such consent has been voluntarily given before such child shall be removed from such reservation. And it shall be unlawful for any Indian agent or other employee of the Government to induce, or seek to induce, by withholding rations or by other improper means, the parents or next of kin of any Indian to consent to the removal of any Indian child beyond the limits of any reservation. (28 Stats., p. 906.) Provided, That hereafter no Indian child shall be taken from any school in any State or Territory to a school in any other State against its will or without the written consent of its parents. (29 Stats., p. 348.) That no Indian pupil under the age of fourteen years shall be transported at Government expense to any Indian school beyond the limits of the State or Territory in which the parents of such child reside or of the adjoining State or Territory. (35 Stat. L., 781.) The rules provide that— A pupil who has been regularly enrolled in a nonreservation school must not be taken to any other nonreservation school without the consent of both superintendents and the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and superintendents will be held to strict accountability for such pupils taken to their schools. An Indian boy or girl 18 years old and over may, without the consent of parents or others, personally sign the application form on its being changed to suit the case; but in all cases where the parents are living they should first be consulted. Compliance must be given to all orders and instructions promulgated in connection with the new course of study issued December 1, 1915. The information as to public school facilities called for in the certificate of the Superintendent (third page hereof) must be given, and all superintendents are especially directed to exhaust every means to secure enrollment of Indian children in the State public schools, pursuant to instructions heretofore issued in this regard. Dear Sir: There is enclosed herewith Official Receipt No. 176061 covering voluntary deposit of $13.88, September 9, 1919. Very respectfully, Superintendent. /MG ENC. Skasaad Alaska Aug 15, 1919 Mr. E.H. Hammond Dept. Cushman Indian School Tacoma Wash. Dear Sir, I received your letter of July 28, and note what you say about my son's action. I was not at all surprised to learn that he had taken French leave, and it is quite likely that he will try the same thing in the future. The letter which you say he wrote has not been received. In fact, he has not written home more than 3 months. It will be necessary for you to keep him under very strict discipline for some time, at least. Does he take any interest in books or his work? I wish you would let me know from time to time how he is getting along. Yours truly, J.L. Johnson Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Aug. 27, 1919 Mr. T. F. Johnson Kasaan, Alaska Dear Mr. Johnson: Your son, Danile Franklin, has been improving both in conduct and application since my last letter. He was returned forcibly to school and was placed in charge of one of the employees who was instructed to keep an eye on him. I am very glad to tell you that Daniel responded to the employee's manner of treatment and really applied himself. He has been doing such good work as painter that I placed him on the payroll this last week to enable him to earn a little spending money for the fair next October. If I could only make Daniel stop chewing tobacco, it would be very much better for him. Very truly yours, Superintendent. EHH:MG Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., July 28, 1919 T. F. Johnson Kasaan, Alaska My dear Mr. Johnson: You have, by this time, received the Official Receipt for the payment of the tuition for the second quarter. Daniel is becoming very fat, but occasionally insists that he has consumption. After the close of school, he and the McAlpin boys left without permission and picked berries in the country for several days before I found them. Daniel was punished reasonably for this misbehavior and wrote you a most heart-rending letter declaring that he was dying of consumption and begging you to send him home. He is, as I have said, becoming very stout and I hope in time he will change his attitude as you know he will benefit very much from the reasonable discipline and the excellent work of industrial instruction given him. If you know of any more boys, fourteen years old, or older, who should be in school, I shall be glad to promise them every opportunity to make good here. Sincerely yours, Superintendent. EHH:MG Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Sept. 22, 1919 Chief of Police Everett, Washington Sir: I have been informed that Daniel Franklin Johnson, a deserter from the Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, is in the vicinity of Everett, Washington. He left school about two weeks ago without permission and has not yet returned. Daniel Franklin Johnson is a half-breed Alaskan Indian, 16 years of age, about five feet tall, medium build, large brown eyes, slow and precise in manner of speaking, and has a peculiar, slouchy walk. If you apprehend him, kindly notify me by wire, at my expense, and detain him until I or my representative arrives for the boy. Thanking you in advance, I am Very respectfully, Superintendent. Kasaan Alaska July 1, 1919 Mr. E. H. Hannum Sept Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash. Dear Sir, Enclosed please find check for $20.00, 1st payment for 3 months tuition; from July 1st until Sept 30, 1919. Yours truly, J. T. G. Johnson OR 176046 File Paul G. Johnson Paul G. Parker 301 Fourth Avenue North Seattle, Washington. Dear Sir: Enclosed herewith find application blank for Daniel Johnson of Kassanq Alaska. Will you kindly fill out the necessary data, giving also the boy's religion if you can and the degree of Indian blood. Thanking you for your early attention in the matter, I am Very sincerely, Asst. Clerk. Capt. Cushman School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Sir: The bearer of this letter, Daniel Johnson, is the son of T. F. Johnson of Kansas Bluff, Idaho. The boy seems to have a bad cold. I fear he is sickful and may not let you know just how badly he feels. I assume that you will have him examined by your school physician and given such care and treatment as he may need. He has never been in school; but he has had a good practical experience, and I find him to be very observing and inquisitive—if he is not afraid. I hope for good results from him. If I can be of any use to him in any way, I hope he or you will let me know. Yours truly, C. H. Parker Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington April 8, 1919. Mr. T. F. Johnson Kasaan, Alaska. Dear Sir: Your son, David Franklin, arrived safely at Cushman. Daniel will naturally feel homesick and will probably consider a return to Alaska any time within the next six months. I shall, however, try to interest him in his work and studies so that he will become attached to the school and will strive to profit by the advantages offered him. If he leaves school without my knowledge or consent, I shall have him traced and brought back until his three year term has expired. The Government charges parents who are able to support their children a tuition fee of $200.00 a year. We have a number of Alaskans whose parents pay their tuition at Cushman. If you are in a position to do so, I advise you to do it as it will undoubtedly exert a good influence over Daniel and encourage him to make the best of his opportunities. Daniel arrived at the school with a bad cold and told me that he did not think he would stay long as he had consumption. I had our doctor examine him immediately and found that his lungs weren't affected in the least degree, so you need not worry if he writes you that he has consumption. It will mean that he is homesick and wishes you to take him out of school. Very truly yours, Superintendent Skasaad Alaska March 20, 1919 Mr. C. H. Hammond Superintendent Cushman School Tacoma, Wash. Dear Sir, I have made arrangements to send my son Daniel T. Johnson to the Cushman School. It is rather late in the season for him to begin, but he will be there, and will be ready for the next season. I want him to remain there during the vacation season. I also want him to remain there for the term of 3 years. Simply let me know what I am expected to pay for his keep, and I will try to meet same quarterly (providing that is acceptable), and I am arranging with Mr. C. L. Parker of Seattle to meet the boy when he arrives at Seattle, and to see that he reaches the school. It may be necessary for you to keep a pretty close watch on the boy, as he may take a notion to leave the school. Yours truly, T. T. Johnson Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., May 6, 1919 T. F. Johnson Kasaan Alaska Dear Sir: Enclosed herewith find Official Receipt No. 131297 for Tuition for Daniel B. Johnson in Cushman Indian School, April 1 to June 30, 1919. Very respectfully, Superintendent. /g Kasaan Alaska 4/25/1919 Mr. E.H. Hammond Superintendent Cushman School Tacoma, Wash. Dear Sir, Your favor of April 8th at hand and contents noted. Enclosed you will please find check for the amount of $2.00. I will send check for $2.00 every three months in future. I note what you say regarding my boy. I don't think he will desire to take him into school, as he would know that I would not do anything of the kind. But he may take the liberty to leave on his own accord some time, so you should not allow him too much liberty. I hope that he will take an interest in his studies and his work as well, so that he may amount to something when he grows up. Yours truly, I.F. Johnston VACATION REQUEST FOR PUPIL. PARKER ATTORNEY AT LAW 301 FOURTH AVENUE NORTH SEATTLE, WASH. April 23, 1919. Supt. Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Sir:- I received letter under date of the 31st ult. from your Assistant Clerk, enclosing application for the enrollment of Daniel Johnson, an Indian boy from Kasaan, Alaska. I could not furnish all the information, so I sent the application to T. F. Johnson, father of the boy, at Kasaan, and it has been returned to me today. I therefore enclose it herewith, with the information furnished by the father. The boy's father and mother are both living. I sincerely hope that the boy will get along well. If I can be of any service to you or the boy, kindly let me know. The father is extremely anxious for the boy to be diligent and to learn. I was especially impressed with the boy's inquisitive nature. I found that he was very observing. Yours truly, C. L. Parker CASE RECORD. NAME Daniel Franklin Johnson Sex Male. FARM ENGINEERING. RECORD CARD—PREVOCATIONAL DIVISION. Each boy should devote 10 weeks to the work of this department during the three prevocational years. When he has accomplished the work as outlined in the course of study in a satisfactory manner, a suitable rating should be recorded. Ratings must be based on a practical application as well as a knowledge of the principles involved. Ratings should be excellent (E), good (G), fair (F). If pupil's work is not worthy of a rating of fair, no grade should be recorded. Under "Remarks" mention anything that indicates interest, conduct, and proficiency of the pupil. This card should be filed in folder for record of pupil (5-197). When the pupil is transferred to another school a copy of this card should be sent to the officer in charge of the school to which he is transferred.
